title: Problem Overview: Distinct Distance Counts
content:
**Erdős Problem #653** studies how the 'distance richness' of individual points varies across a planar configuration. For each point x_i in a set of n points, R(x_i) counts the number of distinct distances from x_i to other points. The function g(n) is the maximum number of distinct R-values achievable by any n-point configuration.

**Conjecture:** g(n) ≥ (1 - o(1))n, meaning almost all points should have different distance-richness levels.

**Known bounds:** 0.7n < g(n) < n - cn^{2/3}

**Status: OPEN**
mathContext: This is a problem in combinatorial geometry related to Erdős's famous distinct distances problem. It measures local distance diversity (per-point) rather than global distance counts.

title: Distance Functions and R(x)
content:
**euclidDist(p, q):** Standard Euclidean distance √((x₁-x₂)² + (y₁-y₂)²) in ℝ².

**distanceSet(S, p):** The set of all distances from p to other points in S, computed as S.filter(· ≠ p).image(euclidDist p).

**distinctDistCount(S, p) = R(xᵢ):** The cardinality of distanceSet, counting how many distinct distances emanate from p.

For example, a point equidistant from all others has R = 1, while a point at distinct distances from every other has R = n-1.
mathContext: R(xᵢ) measures the 'distance richness' or local diversity of point xᵢ. The variation in R across points is what the problem studies.

title: The Function g(n)
content:
**rValueSet(S):** The set {R(x₁), ..., R(xₙ)} of all distance-count values, computed as S.image(distinctDistCount S).

**numDistinctRValues(S):** How many different R-values appear in S.

**g(n):** The supremum of numDistinctRValues over all n-point configurations. This captures the maximum possible 'R-diversity' — how many different distance-richness levels can coexist.

The conjecture asks whether g(n)/n → 1, meaning configurations exist where almost every point has a unique distance-count.
mathContext: g(n) is defined as a supremum, which is natural but means proving lower bounds requires exhibiting specific configurations. The key difficulty is constructing configurations with many distinct R-values.

title: Known Bounds on g(n)
content:
**erdos_fishburn_bound** (axiom): g(n) > 3n/8 for n ≥ 8. The first nontrivial lower bound.

**csizmadia_bound** (axiom): g(n) > 7n/10 for n ≥ 10. The current best lower bound, improving Erdős-Fishburn.

**upper_bound** (axiom): g(n) < n - cn^{2/3} for some c > 0. This shows perfect R-diversity (g = n) is impossible for large n — there must always be some collision among R-values, with the gap growing at least as n^{2/3}.
mathContext: The gap between the 0.7n lower bound and the n - cn^{2/3} upper bound brackets g(n) but leaves the precise asymptotics wide open. The conjecture predicts the lower bound is closer to truth.

title: The Erdős Conjecture (OPEN)
content:
**erdos653Conjecture:** For any ε > 0, there exists N such that for all n ≥ N, g(n) ≥ (1-ε)n.

Equivalently: g(n)/n → 1 as n → ∞. This says that in optimal configurations, almost all points have distinct R-values.

The conjecture remains open. The gap between the 0.7 lower bound and the conjectured limit of 1 is one of the key open questions in combinatorial geometry.
mathContext: If true, this would mean the R-function is 'almost injective' on optimal configurations. The n^{2/3} upper gap prevents full injectivity but allows (1-o(1))-injectivity.

title: Special Configurations: Collinear and Regular Polygon
content:
**IsCollinear(S):** Points lying on a single line. Equally spaced collinear points give varying R-values since endpoints see different distance sets than interior points.

**IsRegularPolygon(S):** Points on a circle at equal spacing. By rotational symmetry, every vertex has the same R-value, giving only g = 1 distinct R-value regardless of n — the worst case.

**regular_polygon_r_value** (axiom): In a regular n-gon (n ≥ 3), all points have the same distinctDistCount. This formalizes the symmetry argument.
mathContext: Regular polygons demonstrate that symmetric configurations are bad for R-diversity. Configurations maximizing g(n) must break symmetry to create varied local distance structures.

title: The Asymptotic Gap n - g(n)
content:
**gap_lower_bound** (axiom): n - g(n) ≥ cn^{2/3} for some c > 0. The gap between n and g(n) is at least of order n^{2/3}.

**gap_bounds** (axiom): For n ≥ 10, cn^{2/3} ≤ n - g(n) ≤ 0.3n. Packages both the n^{2/3} lower bound on the gap and the Csizmadia upper bound.

The conjecture asserts n - g(n) = o(n), meaning the gap is sublinear. The n^{2/3} lower bound on the gap shows it cannot vanish entirely.
mathContext: The gap function n - g(n) is the key quantity. If o(n), the conjecture holds. The n^{2/3} lower bound suggests geometric constraints fundamentally limit R-diversity.

title: Summary Theorems
content:
**erdos_653_summary** (PROVED): Combines three results:
1. ∀ n ≥ 10, g(n) > 7n/10 (Csizmadia lower bound)
2. ∀ n, g(n) ≤ n (trivial upper bound)
3. ∃ c > 0, ∀ n ≥ 2, g(n) < n - cn^{2/3} (nontrivial upper gap)

**erdos_653** (PROVED): Definitionally equal to erdos_653_summary.

Proof: Direct application of csizmadia_bound, g_le_n, and upper_bound axioms via ⟨_, _, _⟩.
mathContext: The summary packages all known quantitative results. The open conjecture (g(n)/n → 1) is stated separately as erdos653Conjecture but not included in the proved summary.
